messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Rajesh

Rajesh was forty-three when his daughter Priya fell ill. She had complained of a sore throat one Tuesday morning, nothing unusual for a child heading into autumn, but by Thursday her fever had climbed past 104 degrees and she lay in the pediatric ward of County General, her small body tethered to machines he did not fully understand. The doctors spoke of meningitis, of a lumbar puncture, of antibiotics. Rajesh, who had spent twenty years defusing ordnance—who had learned to steady his hands while kneeling beside a device that could unmake him in microseconds—found himself unable to steady anything. He watched the neurologist approach with a needle longer than any he had ever seen, watched Priya's face contort as they held her still, and something fractured inside him that he had kept intact through decades of controlled breathing and compartmentalization. For six days she hovered between recovery and catastrophe. When she finally turned the corner, when the fever broke and the antibiotics began to work, Rajesh had already been remade by the helplessness of those hours—by the knowledge that his vigilance, his years of training, his ability to read danger and neutralize it, had meant nothing here. A child's body was not a bomb. You could not defuse illness.

Fifteen years have passed. Priya is healthy now, a college student studying engineering. But Rajesh, at fifty-eight, finds himself trapped in a vigilance that has never truly loosened. He lies awake most nights, his mind refusing to settle into sleep, convinced that some catastrophe is imminent—not just for Priya, but for his wife Meera, for anyone he loves. He is certain that his inability to protect them, demonstrated so thoroughly in that hospital room, means he is fundamentally weak, that he has failed at the most basic requirement of being a man and a father. When he catches himself scanning for threats in ordinary moments—cataloguing exits, listening for the sound of an ambulance—he becomes convinced that his mind is fracturing, that he is losing his grip on reality. These thoughts terrify him more than the original trauma.

Three months ago, Meera developed a routine dental infection. When she mentioned needing to see a specialist, Rajesh felt his chest tighten. The thought of any medical setting, any hospital, sent him spiraling. He declined to accompany her, claiming work obligations, but the real reason was far more shameful: the moment he imagined stepping through those doors again, smelling that particular antiseptic—that sharp, chemical smell that had soaked into his clothes during Priya's hospitalization—his body responded as though the threat were immediate and present. His heart would race, his palms would sweat, and suddenly he was not fifty-eight years old in 2024; he was in that pediatric ward, watching his daughter in agony. The memory came without warning, complete and sensory, as if every nerve ending in his body was reliving that moment. He could see the needle approaching Priya's spine, could hear her crying, could feel the impotence that had hollowed him out.

These intrusions have begun to reshape his life in ways he cannot control. Last month, his team at the bomb disposal unit was called to a school where a suspicious package had been found. Rajesh, who had trained for this work his entire career, found himself unable to focus on the technical problem in front of him. A group of children had been evacuated to a nearby playground, and their presence—their smallness, their vulnerability—triggered the same cascade of memory and dread that the hospital smell had. He saw Priya in every one of them. His hands shook as he worked. His supervisor noticed. Since then, Rajesh has begun to avoid the school calls, volunteering for other assignments, making excuses. His reputation, built over decades, is beginning to crack. At home, he finds himself unable to be in the same room when his grandniece visits; he makes reasons to work late, to stay in the garage. Meera has started to ask questions, hurt and confused by his distance from family, and Rajesh cannot explain to her that being around children now feels like standing at the edge of a precipice—that their presence is a reminder of everything he cannot protect, everything he failed to prevent.

The worst part is the conviction, which has grown harder to shake with each passing week, that his reactions prove something fundamentally broken inside him. A strong man would have moved past this. A capable man would not be haunted by a trauma that happened fifteen years ago, when his daughter survived. He lies awake at three in the morning, his mind cycling through the same thoughts: he is weak, he is going mad, he cannot stop bad things from happening. And because he believes these things about himself, he finds himself more alert, more vigilant, more certain that danger is always seconds away. The vigilance feeds the belief, which feeds the memory, which feeds the conviction that he is coming apart at the seams.

Last week, Rajesh finally made an appointment. He told Meera only that he was having trouble sleeping, but the truth is more complicated and more frightening: he is running out of room inside himself to contain what happened. He is afraid that if he does not find help soon, he will lose not just his career but his family—that the distance he has created between himself and the people he loves will become permanent, and he will have failed them again.

violation_explanations: Triggers (hospital smell, children, medical settings) appear throughout the vignette and negative appraisals (weakness, failure, mind fracturing) are described, but no paragraph explicitly conveys that the triggers themselves drive or lead to the negative appraisals about himself.

Threat perception (sense of imminent catastrophe, danger always seconds away) and triggers (sensory cues, children, medical settings) both appear, but no paragraph shows that the threat conviction directly causes him to encounter or seek out triggering stimuli.
